analysis.one_liner: Doubles the child tax credit, makes it fully refundable, and pays for it by raising the corporate tax rate.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee: referred to Ways and Means on August 13, 2024, it never received a markup or a floor vote before the term ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would raise the child tax credit from $1,000 to $2,000 per child, remove the income limits that phase the credit down and out for higher earners, and make the credit fully refundable — meaning a family gets the full amount even if it owes no income tax, which is what cashes in for single parents and low-wage workers. To pay for it, the bill raises the corporate income tax rate from 21% to 28%. It was referred to the tax-writing committee and never taken up.
analysis.who_benefits: Single parents and low- and moderate-income families with children. The current credit shrinks for families that owe little or no income tax, which is why researchers call the gap a 'single parent penalty'; a fully refundable $2,000 credit means those families get the full amount in cash regardless of tax owed.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Single parents and low-income families with kids

how_it_helps.text: Raises the child tax credit from $1,000 to $2,000 per child [S2].
Repeals the income-based limits on the credit and makes it fully refundable, so families that owe little or no income tax receive the full amount [S2].
Pays for the expansion by raising the corporate income tax rate from 21% to 28%, rather than adding to the deficit [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Corporations, through a permanent increase in the corporate income tax rate from 21% to 28%. Economists debate how much of a corporate tax falls on shareholders versus workers, so some of the cost may reach wages or prices.

drawbacks.text: The seven-percentage-point corporate rate increase is a large permanent tax change; critics of higher corporate rates argue they reduce investment and can lower wages over time, and the bill offers no analysis of that tradeoff [S2].

The expansion is permanent and applies to all income levels once the income limits are repealed, so a significant share of the cost goes to families who would have received a partial credit anyway [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit side is direct and well understood: a fully refundable credit of $2,000 per child sharply reduces child poverty among single-parent and low-wage households. The cost is a substantial permanent corporate tax increase whose incidence is genuinely debated — shareholders bear much of it, but some may fall on workers. The design is straightforward rather than finely tuned; the larger problem is that it never got a hearing, so no one had to defend or amend it.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House tax committee on the day it was introduced and sat there with no markup, no hearing, and no floor vote until the term ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Katie Porter introduced the bill on August 13, 2024, with Reps. Pressley and Ramirez [S1].
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the committee that handles tax bills [S5].
No further action was taken: the committee never marked it up and the House never voted on it before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5].
It drew three cosponsors, all House Democrats [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporations keep the 21% rate, and the current child tax credit's limits stay in place, so single parents and low-income families receive nothing from this proposal. Committee leadership avoided a vote on a corporate tax increase.

for.name: 3 of 216 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Reps. Pressley and Ramirez.

against.name: House Committee on Ways and Means
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Rep. Jason Smith, R-MO)
against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral — no markup, no hearing, no vote — for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All four backers were House Democrats and no Republicans signed on; the Republican-led tax committee took no action on it.

industries.note: The bill would raise their tax rate from 21% to 28% to fund the child credit. Because the bill died in committee, they keep the lower rate; some of the cost of a higher rate would have fallen on shareholders, with a disputed share on wages and prices.

A fully refundable credit delivered directly through the tax code reduces the value of paid-prep and refund-advance products marketed to low-income filers. This is a secondary, unquantified effect; the bill does not address it directly.
